summary.text: Long division is a standard way to divide multi-digit numbers by hand, breaking a division problem into a series of easier steps.
One number, the dividend, is divided by another, the divisor, to give the quotient, and the work starts from the left-most digit of the dividend.
At each step the leftover is carried forward by bringing down the next digit, and the work is complete once all digits are used and no remainder is left.

facts.label: Three parts
facts.value: The dividend is divided by the divisor to give the quotient

facts.label: Short division
facts.value: Almost always used instead when the divisor has one digit

facts.label: Written layout
facts.value: English-speaking countries use a bracket tableau, nicknamed a bus stop

items.prompt: You start dividing 500 by 4 by hand and begin with only the 5. Why not the whole number or the first two digits?

options.label: The 5 is the biggest digit, so it must go first
Four cannot divide 50, so the next digit is skipped
Hand division always starts with a single digit
The 5 is the shortest left-hand stretch of digits that 4 goes into at least once

items.explain: You look for the shortest sequence of digits from the left that the divisor goes into at least once. Here that is just the first digit, 5.

items.prompt: In dividing 500 by 4, the 5 gets used up and 1 is left over. What happens with the next digit, 0?

options.label: It is placed beside the leftover 1 to make 10, which is worked on next
It is added to the 1, giving a total of 1 and starting over
It is put into the quotient immediately as a 0
It is set aside until every other digit has been used

items.explain: The next unused digit is copied next to the remainder 1 to form 10, and the process repeats on that number.

items.prompt: You must divide a large number by a one-digit number like 7 and want less writing. What do people almost always use?

options.label: Long division with the bracket drawn twice
The decimal form with zeros brought down first
Short division, the abbreviated form of long division
Dividing by 7 using the Danda method

items.explain: Short division is the abbreviated form of long division, and it is almost always used when the divisor has only one digit.

items.prompt: Dividing by hand, you reach a step where the digits so far are worth 7 and the divisor is 3. What is written and what happens next?

options.label: Write 2.33 in the quotient and finish at once
Write 2 in the quotient; the leftover 1 is carried forward
Write 3 in the quotient, rounding up, with a leftover of 2
Write 2 in the quotient and discard the leftover 1

items.explain: The quotient at each step is rounded down to an integer, and the remainder is calculated and carried forward to the next digit.

items.prompt: You divided by hand and ended with a leftover, but you want a decimal answer rather than a fraction. How do you continue?

options.label: Round the quotient to the nearest whole number
Extend the dividend with zeros after a decimal point and keep bringing them down
Start again with the divisor and dividend swapped
Multiply the leftover by the divisor and add it on

items.explain: The dividend can be extended by writing it with a decimal point and zeros, and the process continues to give a decimal answer.

items.prompt: A dividend begins with the digit 1 and the divisor is 4. How does the first step go?

options.label: Use the first two digits, since 1 is too small
Divide the 1 by 4 and then carry on in decimals
Start from the right-most digit instead
Switch to short division for that step

items.explain: When the first digit is less than the divisor, the first step is performed on the first two digits.
